title: Your Agent Just Authorized What?! — Jay Mok & Ben Coumes, Paypal
talk_summary: They map Claude Code connectors, shared vaults with OAuth scopes, and FIDO verifiable intents/AP2 mandates onto that matrix, arguing cryptographic proof is only needed for high-stakes, open-ecosystem, hard-to-reverse actions.

takeaways.technique: Stakes × counterparty trust matrix for agent action gating
takeaways.what_they_do: Classify each agent action by stakes and whether the counterparty is inside a trusted boundary; low-stakes reversible actions need only logs, high-stakes irreversible ones need verifiable authorization.
takeaways.evidence_quote: is it a low stakes or high stakes kind of scenario? ... is this a kind of like open ecosystem or closed ecosystem?

takeaways.what_they_do: Authorization tokens carry scope, expiry, and target (merchant/product intent) so authority is bounded rather than all-or-nothing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It's generally going to be a time bound um you know you know token. Um and an amount and possibly could be identified like a merchant

takeaways.technique: Audit trail as the evidence layer for low/medium stakes
takeaways.what_they_do: For closed-ecosystem, reversible actions they rely on existing transaction/system logs rather than cryptographic proof, because disputes can be resolved from logs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they're able to leverage like the just the existing transaction logs

takeaways.technique: Trust boundary via shared intermediary (borrowed trust)
takeaways.what_they_do: Two agents that don't directly trust each other both rely on a shared platform to enforce the mandate, making the ecosystem 'closed' and lowering evidence requirements.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they're borrowing trust from, you know, Nevermind to make sure that, you know, the buying agent is falling within, you know, the instructions that a human has given it
